results.construction: Spec: mode interval, range [-6,6], from -4, to 3, openFrom false, openTo true. Student answer: filled circle at -4 (square bracket, included), hollow circle at 3 (round bracket, excluded). Both endpoints are whole numbers inside the range, the range is 12 wide and within +-20, so every validator limit is met.

predicates.why: Interval mode lists this predicate. It fires when the endpoints sit at -4 and 3 but the circles are wrong. A student holding the swapped-brackets belief reads [ as a strict sign (<) and ) as an inclusive one (<=), so she puts a hollow circle at -4 and a filled circle at 3: right positions, both circles flipped. That is the construction that fires the predicate, and it is what this misconception produces. The predicate would also fire for a one-endpoint slip, but the full flip is a genuine product of this belief.

results.construction: Spec: mode interval, range [-2,10], from 1, to 8, openFrom false, openTo true. The range is widened from the example [-6,6] because 8 must lie inside it. Student answer: filled circle at 1, hollow circle at 8. Both endpoints are whole numbers inside the range, which is 12 wide and within +-20.

predicates.why: Interval mode lists this predicate. The swapped-brackets student reads [ as < and ) as <=, so she places a hollow circle at 1 and a filled circle at 8: endpoints right, both circles wrong. That is the build that fires the predicate and the build this misconception yields.

results.construction: Spec: mode interval, range [-10,2], from -8, to -2, openFrom false, openTo true. Student answer: filled circle at -8, hollow circle at -2. Both endpoints are whole numbers inside the range, which is 12 wide and within +-20. Negative values are allowed.

predicates.why: Interval mode lists this predicate. The swapped-brackets student puts a hollow circle at -8 and a filled circle at -2, with both end numbers right and both circles flipped. That fires the predicate and is exactly what the brackets-swapped-for-signs belief produces.

results.construction: Spec: mode interval, range [-6,8], from -1, to 6, openFrom false, openTo true. Student answer: filled circle at -1, hollow circle at 6. Both endpoints are whole numbers inside the range, which is 14 wide and within +-20.

predicates.why: Interval mode lists this predicate. The swapped-brackets student marks a hollow circle at -1 and a filled circle at 6: right end numbers, both circles flipped. That is the construction that fires the predicate and the one this misconception produces.

results.construction: Spec: mode interval, range [0,12], from 2, to 9, openFrom false, openTo true. Student answer: filled circle at 2, hollow circle at 9. Both endpoints are whole numbers inside the range, which is 12 wide and within +-20.

predicates.why: Interval mode lists this predicate. The swapped-brackets student marks a hollow circle at 2 and a filled circle at 9, so both end numbers are right and both circles are flipped. That fires the predicate and is what this misconception yields.

results.construction: Instrument config range [-10,5] (width 15, whole numbers within +-20, contains -7 and 2). Student taps -7 and sets it hollow (excluded, round bracket), taps 2 and sets it filled (included, square bracket). Interval -7 < x <= 2. Every limit is met.

predicates.why: Interval mode lists this predicate. Firing build: from=-7 and to=2 correct, but -7 filled and 2 hollow (both circles flipped). A student who swaps round and square brackets reads ( as included and ] as excluded, and builds exactly this. The mixed interval (one open, one closed) is where the swap shows as right end numbers with wrong circles, which is the misconception's wording.

results.construction: Instrument config range [-6,8] (width 14, within +-20, contains -3 and 5). Student taps -3 and sets it hollow, taps 5 and sets it filled. Interval -3 < x <= 5. Every limit is met.

predicates.why: Interval mode lists this predicate. Firing build: ends -3 and 5 correct, -3 filled and 5 hollow. That is what a student who has round and square brackets swapped builds when pairing each bracket with a filled or hollow circle (filled = <=, hollow = <). It fires on right end numbers with wrong circles, which is the claimed misconception.

results.construction: Instrument config range [-3,10] (width 13, within +-20, contains 0 and 7). Student taps 0 and sets it hollow, taps 7 and sets it filled. Interval 0 < x <= 7. Every limit is met.

predicates.why: Interval mode lists this predicate. Firing build: ends 0 and 7 correct, 0 filled and 7 hollow. A student with round and square brackets swapped reads ( as included and ] as excluded and so flips both circles. The ends are right and only the inclusion is wrong, which matches the stated misconception.

results.construction: Instrument config range [-12,0] (width 12, within +-20, contains -9 and -4). Student taps -9 and sets it hollow, taps -4 and sets it filled. Interval -9 < x <= -4. Every limit is met.

predicates.why: Interval mode lists this predicate. Firing build: ends -9 and -4 correct, -9 filled and -4 hollow. This is the picture a student with round and square brackets swapped produces for (-9, -4]. The end numbers are right but the inclusion is wrong at both ends, as the misconception describes.

results.construction: Rearrange 2y = x - 4 to y = x/2 - 2, so m = 1/2 and b = -2. Both are allowed (1/2 is the reciprocal of the whole number 2, and |m| <= 5; b = -2 is within -5..5). Drag the two handles to the lattice points (0,-2) and (4,0). Both sit on the line, they are distinct, and neither is at the opening handle positions (-3,-2) or (1,1). The live equation reads y = 0.5x - 2, which is the target. Other valid pairs include (2,-1) with (-2,-3) and (-4,-4) with (4,0).

predicates.why: This predicate fires on a line with slope 1/2 and an intercept other than -2, such as y = x/2 - 4 through (0,-4) and (4,-2). A student with this misconception reads the gradient straight off the x-term of 2y = x - 4 and gets m = 1, not 1/2, so her slope is wrong as well. Her line y = x - 4 has both slope and intercept wrong. Keeping the right slope while botching only the constant would mean dividing the x-term by 2 but not the constant, which is a different, partial-division error. So intercept-wrong would mostly fire for that other mistake and not for this one.

The student reads m = 1 from the x-term and takes the constant -4 as printed, so she builds y = x - 4, for example by dragging to (0,-4) and (4,0). Her slope 1 is not 1/2, and her intercept -4 is not -2. Her slope is not the sign-flipped value -1/2 or the inverted value 2, and the line is not vertical, so none of the specific equation-mode predicates fires. Only the catch-all 'neither the slope nor the intercept matches' fires, and this is exactly the build this misconception produces. off-target is listed for equation mode.

results.construction: Rearranging y + 3 = 2x gives y = 2x - 3, so m = 2 and b = -3 (a whole number inside -5..5, with |m| <= 5, so within the instrument's limits). In equation mode any two points on the line are accepted. Drag the two handles to the lattice points (0, -3) and (2, 1). Check: 2*0 - 3 = -3 and 2*2 - 3 = 1. Both lie in the +/-5 grid. Neither is a starting handle position, (-3, -2) or (1, 1), and neither starting position is on the line, so both handles must be moved. (1, -1) and (3, 3) would also work.

predicates.why: The predicate fires when the slope is 2 but the intercept is not -3. A student who reads the 3 beside y as the y-intercept without flipping its sign draws y = 2x + 3. Her handles go to (0, 3) and (1, 5), or (-1, 1) and (1, 5). That line has slope 2 and intercept +3, so it is parallel to the answer and fires intercept-wrong. The slope comes straight from the 2x term, so the sign slip changes only the intercept. For this equation it is the natural way to get the right slope with the wrong intercept. The equation-mode can_emit list includes intercept-wrong, so it can fire.

A student who swaps gradient and intercept reads the 3 as the gradient and the 2 as the intercept. Reading the rearranged form y = 2x - 3 the same way gives gradient -3 and intercept 2. The built line is y = 3x + 2 (handles at (0, 2) and (1, 5)) or y = -3x + 2 (handles at (0, 2) and (1, -1)). Both are reachable on the grid. The slope (3 or -3) is not 2, and the intercept (2) is not -3, so neither matches. The vertical-line, slope-sign-flipped (slope -2) and slope-inverted (slope 1/2) tests do not fire, and neither does intercept-wrong, which needs slope 2. That leaves off-target, which is in the equation-mode can_emit list. It is a catch-all, but the swap lands in it for certain and not in any more specific predicate.

results.construction: Rearranged, y + 2x = 4 is y = -2x + 4, so m = -2 and b = 4. Both are legal for the instrument (whole-number m with |m| <= 5, whole b in -5..5). The intercepts are found by setting x = 0 (giving y = 4) and y = 0 (giving x = 2). Drag handle 1 to the lattice point (0, 4) and handle 2 to (2, 0). Both lie on the line, both are within +/-5, and neither is at the starting handle positions (-3, -2) or (1, 1). The line through them has gradient (0-4)/(2-0) = -2 and y-intercept 4, so the live equation reads y = -2x + 4. Other valid pairs are (1, 2) and (3, -2).

predicates.why: Fires on a line with gradient +2 instead of -2, for example the upward line through (0, 4) and (-2, 0), which leans the other way. A student who reads direction from the sign beside x as written sees +2x and expects an increasing graph, so she builds exactly this upward line with the right steepness. The misconception and the predicate describe the same build. Equation mode lists this predicate in can_emit.

Fires on a line with gradient -1/2 instead of -2. A student who puts y = 0 to get the 'y-intercept' (x = 2) and x = 0 to get the 'x-intercept' (y = 4) plots (0, 2) and (4, 0). The line through those points has gradient -1/2, the reciprocal of -2 with the same sign, so the predicate fires. A line through swapped intercepts always has the reciprocal gradient. The question tells the student to find the axis crossings first, so this swap is the likely source of a -1/2 line here, rather than a run-over-rise slip. Equation mode lists this predicate in can_emit. The predicate's wording (run over rise) names the gradient result, not her swapped intercept rule, so the remediation attached to the misconception is the right one.

results.construction: One continuous freehand stroke tracing y = -x^2 + 3, drawn left to right so it never doubles back. Start where the curve enters the grid at the bottom left, about (-2.8, -4.8). Pass through the lattice points (-2, -1), (-1, 2), (0, 3), (1, 2), (2, -1), then finish at the bottom right, about (2.8, -4.8). This is an inverted U with its peak at (0, 3), symmetric about the y-axis, crossing the x-axis at about +/-1.73. The stroke is single-valued in x, so it passes the vertical line test. The coefficients [-1, 0, 3] are within the +/-10 limit and a is not 0. One caveat: the parabola leaves the -5..5 window at |x| of about 2.83, because y reaches -5 there. The instrument says to keep the curve mostly inside -5..5, so I read 'runs right across the grid' as covering the whole visible part of the curve. That is edge to edge of the parabola inside the window, not the full x range -5..5. I read the target as reachable on that basis.

predicates.why: Quadratic can emit this predicate. The q-ignored student draws y = -x^2: an inverted U with its vertex at the origin, the same shape as the target. It sits exactly 3 units below the true curve at every x, which is more than the one-square tolerance. That is a right shape with a consistent vertical offset, which is what this predicate fires on. The wrong construction is the diagnosed misconception, since the student has kept the ax^2 part and dropped +3.

Quadratic can emit this predicate, and the question gives a = -1, so the correct curve opens downward. A student who ignores the sign of a, or reads -x^2 as (-x)^2, draws an upward U such as y = x^2 + 3 or y = x^2. Its concavity is opposite to the target, so the sign-of-a check fires. That is the diagnosed misconception, and a student who picks an upward parabola when a is negative builds exactly this curve.

results.construction: Target y = 2x^2 - 4 (a=2, b=0, c=-4; every coefficient is within the +/-10 limit and a is non-zero). Draw ONE left-to-right stroke that never doubles back: start at the top edge near (-2.1, 5), pass through the lattice points (-2, 4), (-1, -2), then the turning point (0, -4), then (1, -2), (2, 4), and finish near (2.1, 5). Each of these lattice points lies exactly on the curve (2(1)-4=-2, 2(4)-4=4). The vertex at y=-4 is inside -5..5, and the curve only leaves the grid through the top at |x| of about 2.12, so the whole visible portion is drawn. It is a single-valued function, so it passes the vertical line test. The target is reachable. The only caveat is that 'right across the grid' has to mean across the visible part of the curve (about x=-2.1 to 2.1), because the parabola is off the top of the grid beyond that.

predicates.why: Listed in can_emit for quadratic. It fires on an upward-opening parabola with the vertex near (0,-4) but the wrong width, for example y = x^2 - 4 through (+/-1,-3), (+/-2,0), or y = 0.5x^2 - 4, or a narrower y = 4x^2 - 4. These miss the target by 2 to 6 squares away from the vertex, so they exceed the one-square tolerance. Because the miss is not a constant offset, vertically-displaced does not fire, and because the curve opens up, opens-wrong-way does not fire. That is exactly the 'wrong steepness, right direction' sketch described for a student who reads a bigger a as flatter, or who drops the factor 2. Off-target is also the catch-all for other gross misses, but for this question steepness is the dominant way to land there.

Listed in can_emit for quadratic. A student who ignores q draws the origin-vertex parabola y = 2x^2: the correct width and direction, with the vertex at (0,0) through (+/-1,2) and (+/-2,8). It sits a constant 4 squares above the true curve at every x. That is a consistent vertical offset, which is what this predicate detects, and it is what the q-ignored description says the student builds. At most it might also trip partial-coverage, because y=2x^2 leaves the top of the grid at |x| of about 1.58 instead of 2.12, but the displacement signature is the clear one.

Listed in can_emit for quadratic. Here a = +2, so the target opens upward. The predicate fires on a downward-opening sketch, for example a cap with its top at (0,-4) or at (0,4). The misconception text covers this case ('downward when a is positive', sign read the wrong way round). A student who attaches the minus in '-4' to the parabola and flips it is also misreading the sign that controls direction, and a refutation that says 'a is +2 so it opens up, and the -4 only slides it down' fits that student too. The 'ignored' branch of the misconception would simply give an upward curve for a positive a, so it does not apply to this item, but the 'read the wrong way round' branch does.

results.construction: Draw one left-to-right stroke along y = -0.5x^2 + 4 (a=-0.5, b=0, c=4). The vertex is at (0,4) and the curve opens downward. It crosses the x-axis at x = ±2.83 (about ±2.8). Lattice-point samples: (-4,-4), (-3,-0.5), (-2,2), (-1,3.5), (0,4), (1,3.5), (2,2), (3,-0.5), (4,-4). The curve meets the bottom edge y=-5 at x ≈ ±4.24, so extend the stroke to about (-4.2,-4.8) and (4.2,-4.8). It is single-valued in x, so it passes the vertical line test. It covers almost the full width of the grid, and the only part left out is the end that leaves the grid at the bottom. It is within one grid square of the target everywhere. Coefficients are within ±10 and a is not 0, so this is reachable.

predicates.why: Quadratic can emit off-target. Steepness-of-a-misjudged is a parabola that opens downward with its vertex at (0,4) but is wrong in width, for example a=-1 (a bigger |a| read as flatter, drawn through (±2,0), (±3,-5)) or a=-0.2. That curve is right in sign and vertex but drifts from the target by more than one grid square in the arms (2 squares at x=±2). The offset is not constant, so vertically-displaced does not fit. The sign is correct, so opens-wrong-way does not fit. The only generic fallback left is off-target, which is the intended catch for this error.

Quadratic can emit opens-wrong-way. A student who ignores the sign of a draws an upward-opening U (a=+0.5, with a vertex at (0,4) or at (0,-4)). That is the reverse curvature of the target, which is exactly what this predicate detects. The misconception (sign of a ignored or read the wrong way) and the predicate (curvature sign opposite to the target) describe the same error.

Quadratic can emit vertically-displaced. A student who leaves out q draws y = -0.5x^2, with the turning point at the origin. This has the right shape and the right opening direction, and it sits a constant 4 units (4 grid squares) below the target everywhere, which is exactly 'consistently above or below the true curve'. Dropping q is the only mistake that produces a pure vertical shift here, so the predicate fires for this error and not for others. The shifted curve leaves the grid sooner (at x ≈ ±3.2, against ±4.24 for the target), so partial-coverage could in principle also fire. The consistent offset of 4 is the signature, though, so the diagnosis still fits.

results.construction: Solve 2x^2 - 18 = 0, so x^2 = 9 and x = -3 or x = 3. On the points-mode number line with range [-6,6], tap the whole numbers -3 and 3 and nothing else. Both are whole numbers inside the range, and the set {-3, 3} equals the target set exactly.

predicates.why: Question is points mode, and can_emit lists missed-values for points mode. The construction that fires it is the student tapping only 3, a strict subset of {-3, 3} with no extra marks. That is what a student who takes the square root of x^2 = 9 and writes only the positive value builds (mc:g10m4s6-1-3:only-positive-root): they isolate x^2 = 9, write x = 3, and drop -3. The predicate could also fire for other omissions, such as tapping only -3, but the positive-root-only construction is the dominant error and it fires this predicate with no extra marks, so the diagnosis fits.

results.construction: xy=-6 is y=-6/x, so a=-6, q=0 (inside |a|<=6, |q|<=3). Stroke 1, drawn in quadrant II and never touching x=0: (-5,1.2) -> (-4,1.5) -> (-3,2) -> (-2,3) -> (-1.5,4) -> (-1.2,5), hugging the x-axis on the left and rising steeply along the y-axis. The lattice points (-6,1), (-3,2), (-2,3) are on it. Lift the finger. Stroke 2, drawn in quadrant IV: (1.2,-5) -> (1.5,-4) -> (2,-3) -> (3,-2) -> (4,-1.5) -> (5,-1.2), hugging the y-axis on the way down and the x-axis on the right. The lattice points (6,-1), (3,-2), (2,-3) are on it. Neither stroke touches or crosses an axis, the two strokes are separate, and the whole curve stays mostly inside -5..5, so it scores within one grid square.

predicates.why: Fired by a stroke that runs through x=0, for example one stroke from (-3,2) up to the y-axis, across it, and down to (3,-2), or a branch that reaches and touches the axis. This is what a student who thinks the graph eventually meets or crosses its asymptote would draw: she turns 'gets closer to' into 'arrives at', so the branch reaches or passes the line x=0. The instrument's own description of this predicate says an asymptote is a boundary the curve approaches and never crosses, which is the refutation this student needs.

Fired by drawing the branches in quadrants I and III, the shape of xy=+6, instead of II and IV. sign-lost-testing-point is a point-membership checking error, where (-2,3) gives 6 instead of -6 and the student rejects a point that is on the graph. It never produces a sketch. It does not explain putting the whole curve in I and III, where the product is positive and the equation says -6 anyway. A quadrant swap would mostly come from ignoring the minus in -6 or confusing the sign of a. This pairing would refute a mistake the student did not make.

results.construction: xy=-4 is y=-4/x, so a=-4, q=0. Stroke 1, drawn in quadrant II: (-5,0.8) -> (-4,1) -> (-3,1.33) -> (-2,2) -> (-1,4) -> (-0.8,5). The lattice points (-4,1), (-2,2), (-1,4) are on it. Lift the finger. Stroke 2, drawn in quadrant IV: (0.8,-5) -> (1,-4) -> (2,-2) -> (3,-1.33) -> (4,-1) -> (5,-0.8). The lattice points (4,-1), (2,-2), (1,-4) are on it. Each branch approaches both axes without touching or crossing them, and all lattice points are inside -5..5.

predicates.why: Fired by a stroke that passes through x=0, for example from (-2,2) across the y-axis to (2,-2), or a branch drawn onto the axis. A student who believes a graph eventually meets or crosses its asymptote would draw exactly this, with the curve reaching or passing the line x=0 rather than only approaching it. The misconception's refutation (the curve gets closer but never arrives) fits.

Fired by branches in quadrants I and III, the shape of xy=+4. sign-lost-testing-point is an arithmetic slip when testing a point, a negative times a positive being read as positive, so the student wrongly rejects a point on the graph. It does not lead her to draw the curve in the wrong pair of quadrants. That error would mostly come from dropping the negative in -4 or misreading the sign of a, so the diagnosis would mostly fire for a different reason. The misconception text also quotes xy=-6, not this question's xy=-4.

results.construction: xy=-3 is y=-3/x, so a=-3, q=0. Stroke 1, drawn in quadrant II: (-5,0.6) -> (-3,1) -> (-2,1.5) -> (-1,3) -> (-0.6,5). The lattice points (-3,1), (-1,3) are on it. Lift the finger. Stroke 2, drawn in quadrant IV: (0.6,-5) -> (1,-3) -> (2,-1.5) -> (3,-1) -> (5,-0.6). The lattice points (3,-1), (1,-3) are on it. The branches approach both axes without touching or crossing them, are separate strokes, and stay inside -5..5.

predicates.why: Fired by a stroke through x=0, for example a single stroke from (-1,3) across the y-axis to (1,-3), or a branch that touches the axis. This is how a student who thinks a graph eventually meets or crosses its asymptote would draw it, with 'approaches' read as 'arrives at'. The refutation (a boundary the curve approaches and never crosses) fits.

Fired by branches in quadrants I and III, the xy=+3 shape. sign-lost-testing-point is an error in checking whether a point is on the graph (the sign of -2 times 3 is lost) and does not generate a sketch. The student who loses a sign when testing a point does not thereby choose quadrants I and III for the curve. A swap like that would mostly come from ignoring the minus sign in -3 or misreading the sign of a. The misconception text also quotes xy=-6, not this question's xy=-3.

results.construction: y=4/x, so a=4 and q=0. Two strokes, finger lifted between them, neither crossing x=0. Stroke 1 (first quadrant): (0.8,5), (1,4), (1.33,3), (2,2), (3,1.33), (4,1), (5,0.8). Stroke 2 (third quadrant, the mirror through the origin): (-5,-0.8), (-4,-1), (-3,-1.33), (-2,-2), (-1.33,-3), (-1,-4), (-0.8,-5). The exact lattice points (1,4), (2,2), (4,1) and their negatives lie on the curve, and the whole curve fits inside -5..5, so it is within about one grid square everywhere.

predicates.why: Fires when the two branches sit in the second and fourth quadrants. For a=4 that means two strokes through points like (-1,4), (-2,2), (-4,1) and (1,-4), (2,-2), (4,-1), which is y=-4/x. That is exactly the 'second and fourth quadrants for a positive a' construction the sign-of-a-ignored misconception describes. The student gets the shape and distance right and misses only the sign. wrong-quadrants is in the hyperbola can_emit list.

off-target is a direction-blind catch-all, 'the sketch does not follow the curve'. The firing construction is right quadrants, hyperbola shape, but displaced more than about one grid square, for example hugging the axes through (1,1) instead of (2,2). A bigger-a-closer-to-axes student would build that, but so would a student who ignores a and draws y=1/x, a student who draws the branches too far from the axes, and any loose freehand sketch. Too-far curves are the opposite of this misconception, and the predicate cannot tell the two directions apart. It would mostly fire for other reasons and could serve the refutation of a mistake the student did not make. It is in the hyperbola can_emit list, but the match is not specific enough.

results.construction: y=6/x, so a=6 and q=0 (|a|<=6 and whole, allowed). Two strokes, finger lifted, neither crossing x=0. Stroke 1 (first quadrant): (1.2,5), (1.5,4), (2,3), (3,2), (4,1.5), (5,1.2). Stroke 2 (third quadrant): (-5,-1.2), (-4,-1.5), (-3,-2), (-2,-3), (-1.5,-4), (-1.2,-5). The lattice points (2,3), (3,2) and their negatives lie on the curve. (1,6) and (6,1) fall outside -5..5, so the strokes leave the window near the asymptotes, which the 'mostly inside -5..5' guidance allows. The target is reachable within about one grid square.

predicates.why: Fires when the branches are drawn in the second and fourth quadrants, for example through (-2,3), (-3,2) and (2,-3), (3,-2), which is y=-6/x. For a positive a=6 that is the sign-of-a-ignored error in the exact form the misconception states. It is the only possible cause of a correct-shape curve in the wrong pair of quadrants. wrong-quadrants is in the hyperbola can_emit list.

This is the same direction-blind catch-all, 'the sketch does not follow the curve'. A curve hugging the axes (diagonal point near (1.2,1.2) instead of about (2.45,2.45)) fires it, and that is what the bigger-a-closer student would draw. But so would the y=1/x drawn by a student who ignores a, a curve drawn too far out (the opposite of the misconception), or plain freehand imprecision. It would mostly fire for other reasons and could serve the refutation of a mistake the student did not make, so the match is false.

results.construction: y=5/x, so a=5 and q=0. Two strokes, finger lifted, neither crossing x=0. Stroke 1 (first quadrant): (1,5), (1.25,4), (2,2.5), (2.5,2), (4,1.25), (5,1). Stroke 2 (third quadrant): (-5,-1), (-4,-1.25), (-2.5,-2), (-2,-2.5), (-1.25,-4), (-1,-5). The lattice points (1,5), (5,1) and their negatives lie exactly on the curve, and the rest of the curve sits within about one grid square of the other points. It all fits inside -5..5.

predicates.why: Fires when the two branches are drawn in the second and fourth quadrants, for example through (-1,5), (-2,2.5), (-5,1) and (1,-5), (2,-2.5), (5,-1), which is y=-5/x. For a positive a=5 that is exactly 'a graph in the second and fourth quadrants for a positive a', the sign-of-a-ignored error. Shape and distance are right and only the sign is lost. wrong-quadrants is in the hyperbola can_emit list.

off-target is a catch-all, 'the sketch does not follow the curve', and it does not know the direction of the error. A curve hugging the axes (through about (1,1) instead of (2.24,2.24)) fires it, and the bigger-a-closer-to-axes student would draw that. So would a student who ignores a and draws y=1/x, a student who draws the branches too far out (the opposite of this misconception), and any sloppy or imprecise sketch. Most firings would come from other causes, and a student told she read the size of a backwards would be given a mistake she did not make. The match is false.

results.construction: xy = 3 + x rearranges to y = 1 + 3/x, so a = 3, q = 1, asymptotes x = 0 and y = 1. Right branch (x > 0, above y = 1, upper-right of the asymptote crossing): lattice points (1,4), (3,2), plus (0.75,5), (1.5,3), (5,1.6), drawn as one stroke bending down toward y = 1 and up toward x = 0 without touching either. Lift the finger. Left branch (x < 0, below y = 1, lower-left): (-0.6,-4), (-1,-2), (-3,0), (-5,0.4), one stroke dropping toward x = 0 from the left and flattening toward y = 1 from below. Both branches stay inside -5..5, neither crosses x = 0, so the asymptote, orientation and level are all right.

predicates.why: Asymptote-sign-flipped here means drawing y = -1 + 3/x. That is the right orientation (a > 0, branches on the same sides of the asymptotes) but the whole curve sits 2 units below the true one, more than the one-grid-square tolerance. A student who gets the 3 and the size of the 1 right but flips its sign draws exactly this, so the predicate fires for this error. hyperbola lists vertically-displaced in can_emit.

With a = +3 the branches must sit in the upper-right and lower-left of the asymptote crossing. A student who ignores the sign of a draws the mirrored pair (upper-left and lower-right), which is the wrong pair for a positive a. That is the claimed misconception, and hyperbola lists wrong-quadrants.

The predicate fires when one stroke runs through x = 0 (the vertical asymptote), for example joining (-1,-2) to (1,4) in a single line. A student who thinks a graph reaches or crosses its asymptote draws that, even though the question says to lift the finger between branches. Other causes are possible (joining plotted points), but crossing an asymptote is the act the predicate detects and the misconception describes. hyperbola lists asymptote-crossed.

results.construction: xy = 4 + x rearranges to y = 1 + 4/x, so a = 4, q = 1, asymptotes x = 0 and y = 1. Right branch (x > 0, above y = 1): lattice points (1,5), (2,3), (4,2), plus (5,1.8), one stroke that bends toward x = 0 on the way up and toward y = 1 on the way right. Lift the finger. Left branch (x < 0, below y = 1): (-0.8,-4), (-1,-3), (-2,-1), (-4,0), (-5,0.2), one stroke. It stays left of x = 0 and below y = 1, inside -5..5, and does not cross either asymptote. Correct.

predicates.why: A sign slip on the horizontal asymptote gives y = -1 + 4/x. That is the right orientation and shape, 2 units below the true curve, which is beyond the tolerance, so the predicate fires. It is what the asymptote-sign-flipped student builds. hyperbola lists vertically-displaced.

a = +4, so the branches belong in the upper-right and lower-left of the asymptote crossing. Ignoring the sign of a gives the mirror image (upper-left and lower-right), the wrong pair. That is the sign-of-a-ignored error. hyperbola lists wrong-quadrants.

A single stroke passing through x = 0, for example from (-1,-3) up to (1,5), triggers it. A student who believes a graph eventually crosses its asymptote draws this despite the instruction to lift the finger. The same stroke could come from joining points, but crossing the asymptote is what it detects and what the misconception is about. hyperbola lists asymptote-crossed.

results.construction: xy = -3 + x rearranges to y = 1 - 3/x, so a = -3, q = 1, asymptotes x = 0 and y = 1. Right branch (x > 0, below y = 1, lower-right of the asymptote crossing): lattice points (1,-2), (3,0), plus (0.75,-3), (1.5,-1), (5,0.4), one stroke dropping toward x = 0 from the right and flattening toward y = 1 from below. Lift the finger. Left branch (x < 0, above y = 1, upper-left): (-0.75,5), (-1,4), (-3,2), (-5,1.6), one stroke rising toward x = 0 from the left and flattening toward y = 1 from above. All inside -5..5, no asymptote crossed. Correct.

predicates.why: Flipping the sign of the added 1 gives y = -1 - 3/x. It has the right orientation (upper-left and lower-right) but sits 2 units below the true curve, beyond the tolerance. That is the asymptote-sign-flipped build, so the predicate fires. hyperbola lists vertically-displaced.

a = -3, so the branches belong in the upper-left and lower-right of the asymptote crossing. A student who ignores the sign of a draws the positive-a pair (upper-right and lower-left), the wrong pair for a negative a. That is the sign-of-a-ignored error. hyperbola lists wrong-quadrants.

One stroke running through x = 0, for example from (-1,4) down to (1,-2), triggers it. A student who thinks a graph reaches or crosses its asymptote produces that stroke. Joining points is another possible cause, but the stroke crosses the vertical asymptote, which is the error described. hyperbola lists asymptote-crossed.

results.construction: Draw y = 2^x as one left-to-right stroke over the whole grid. Start at the far left at about (-5, 0.03), just above the x-axis. Pass through (-3, 0.125), (-2, 0.25) and (-1, 0.5), staying above y = 0 the whole way. Then cross the y-axis at (0, 1), go through the lattice points (1, 2) and (2, 4), and end near (2.3, 5) at the top of the grid. The left tail hugs y = 0 without touching or crossing it, and the stroke is a single-valued function of x, so it passes the vertical line test. The parameters are in range: a = 1 is a nonzero whole number, b = 2 is in {2, 3, 0.5}, and q = 0. The curve sits inside -5..5 apart from the far left tail, which is nearly flat on the axis, so the target is reachable within one grid square.

predicates.why: For an exponential, asymptote-crossed fires when the stroke dips below or crosses the horizontal asymptote y = q, here the x-axis. It is in the can_emit list for exponential, so it can fire. The claimed misconception is different: the student sees the graphs of y = 2^x and y = 2^-x or y = -2^x as reflections that both hug the x-axis, and so calls the x-axis an axis of symmetry. That is a mislabelling of the axis. It does not produce a single stroke that runs through y = 0. A student who really believed the x-axis was a mirror line would draw the mirror image below it, as a second curve or a doubled-back stroke. That would fail the vertical line test or partial-coverage, not asymptote-crossed. A stroke that crosses the axis comes from thinking the curve can reach zero and carry on into negative y, as a polynomial would, or from drawing carelessly. That is a different reason, so the diagnosis would serve the refutation of a mistake the student did not make.

results.construction: The target is g(x) = 2^(-x) = (1/2)^x, so fn = exponential with a=1, b=0.5, q=0. The validator accepts it: a is a nonzero whole number with |a|<=3, b=0.5 is in {2,3,0.5}, and q=0 is whole with |q|<=3. One stroke, left to right: enter at the top edge near (-2.3, 5), then pass through (-2, 4), (-1, 2) and (0, 1) (the true y-intercept). Continue through (1, 0.5), (2, 0.25) and (3, 0.125), then run along just above the x-axis to (5, ~0.03). The stroke is a single-valued function of x, so it passes the vertical line test. It never crosses the asymptote y=0. It covers every visible x from about -2.3 to 5. Left of x=-2.3 the true curve is off the grid (2^5 = 32 at x=-5), which is the 'mostly inside -5..5' allowance. Near the steep left end the 'within about one grid square' tolerance is easy to meet.

predicates.why: The exponential case lists wrong-intercept in can_emit, and the true y-intercept here is (0, a+q) = (0, 1). A student with reflection-axes-swapped puts the minus sign on the whole function and draws -2^x, the reflection in the x-axis. That curve decreases from near 0 at the left to far below the axis at the right and crosses x=0 at y=-1, 2 units from the true intercept and well outside a one-square tolerance, so the predicate fires. The other builds that miss (0,1) are rarer and less likely: -2^(-x), or a shape pinned to the wrong point. The no-reflection build 2^x keeps the intercept at (0,1) and does not fire it. So this predicate fires mainly for the sign-on-the-whole-function error the misconception describes.

results.construction: The question reads as y = -(2^x) + 3, so a = -1, b = 2, q = 3 (all inside the exponential limits: a nonzero whole with |a|<=3, b in {2,3,0.5}, q whole with |q|<=3). The asymptote is y = 3, the curve lies entirely below it and is decreasing, and the y-intercept is -1 + 3 = 2. Draw one left-to-right stroke through (-5, 3) (the true value is 2.97), (-4, 2.94), (-3, 2.88), (-2, 2.75), (-1, 2.5), (0, 2), (1, 1), (2, -1), then down to (3, -5) where it leaves the bottom of the grid. The stroke hugs y = 3 on the far left without touching or crossing it, passes through (0, 2), and is a function (single-valued in x). Every point is within a grid square of the true curve. The curve exits the grid at x = 3, so coverage runs from the left edge to where the curve leaves the grid, not the whole x-range.

predicates.why: A student who picks the curve from 2^x alone and drops the minus sign draws an increasing curve. The usual version is y = 2^x + 3, which meets the y-axis at (0, 4). The bare 2^x gives (0, 1). Neither is the true intercept (0, 2). The construction that fires the predicate is a stroke that misses (0, 2) by more than the tolerance, and this misconception produces exactly that. The curve sits on the wrong side of the asymptote, so the intercept is the first thing it gets wrong. Exponential is a family where wrong-intercept is emittable.

The predicate fires when the stroke passes through the asymptote y = 3, with points on both sides of it. A student who leaves out a and draws 2^x + 3 has a curve that lies wholly above y = 3 and never crosses it. They have chosen the wrong side of the asymptote, which is a different thing from crossing it. A stroke that does cross y = 3 comes from a student who forgot the shift q (plain 2^x passes y = 3 near x = 1.6), who ignored the asymptote, or who wobbled across it. None of those is this misconception, so the predicate would mostly fire for a different reason.

results.construction: Freehand, one stroke left to right over 0..360 degrees: (0,-1), (45,-2.41), (90,-3), (135,-2.41), (180,-1), (225,0.41), (270,1), (315,0.41), (360,-1). Midline y=-1, amplitude 2, inverted (starts at the midline and falls first), one full period. The range -3..1 sits inside -5..5. The a>0 sine, the wrong midline and the wrong amplitude are all excluded.

predicates.why: The predicate fires on a correct-shape, correct-amplitude, inverted sine whose midline is not y=-1. A student with stretch-applied-to-shift shifts sin θ down 1, then multiplies by -2, giving -2 sin θ + 2: midline y=+2, range 0..4, amplitude 2 and inversion both correct. That construction has the wrong midline and nothing else wrong. Here a·q = 2, which differs from q = -1, so the misconception produces a distinct wrong midline. It is also different from a sign slip on q (midline +1) or ignoring q (midline 0), so the diagnosis fits.

results.construction: Freehand, one stroke left to right: (0,-1), (45,-3.12), (90,-4), (135,-3.12), (180,-1), (225,1.12), (270,2), (315,1.12), (360,-1). Midline y=-1, amplitude 3, inverted, one period. The range -4..2 sits inside -5..5.

predicates.why: A student with stretch-applied-to-shift draws -3(sin θ - 1) = -3 sin θ + 3: midline y=+3, amplitude 3, inverted, range 0..6. Because a·q = 3 differs from q = -1, the midline is clearly wrong while amplitude and orientation are right, so the predicate fires and it fires for this reason. Caveat: the peak of that wrong curve (y up to 6, over roughly 222 to 318 degrees) runs off a -5..5 canvas. A student would draw it clipped near the top edge; the visible midline is still about +2.5 to +3, far from -1, so the predicate still fires. If she notices it does not fit, she self-corrects and no diagnosis is issued, so no wrong diagnosis is served.

results.construction: Freehand, one stroke left to right: (0,-2), (45,-2.71), (90,-3), (135,-2.71), (180,-2), (225,-1.29), (270,-1), (315,-1.29), (360,-2). Midline y=-2, amplitude 1, inverted, one period. The range -3..-1 sits inside -5..5. It is buildable, but with amplitude 1 and a tolerance of about one grid square, the shape check is weak.

predicates.why: Here a = -1, so a·q = +2 is exactly -q. The midline-at-+2 sketch (-sin θ + 2) fires the predicate, but it is the same sketch a student produces from a plain sign slip on the shift. It is also what she draws by reflecting the whole shifted graph in the x-axis. With |a| = 1 there is no stretch for the shift to be multiplied by, so the sketch cannot show the stretch-applied-to-shift reasoning and would mostly fire for a different reason. Serving 'you multiplied the shift by a' to a student who made a sign slip would refute a mistake she did not make.

results.construction: Target y = 3 sin(theta) + 1 on 0..360 degrees: midline y = 1, amplitude 3, so the range is -2..4. Key points, drawn left to right in one stroke: (0,1) rising, (90,4) peak, (180,1) back on the midline, (270,-2) trough, (360,1). Coefficients [3,1] are inside the sine limits (a nonzero whole, |a|<=4; q whole, |q|<=3), and the whole curve fits inside -5..5. It is a single-valued stroke, so it passes the vertical line test.

predicates.why: fn is sine, so vertical-shift-wrong is in the can_emit list. A student who reads 3 sin(theta) + 1 as 3(sin(theta) + 1) shifts first and then stretches. She draws a full-amplitude sine centred on y = a*q = 3 instead of y = 1: (0,3), (90,6), (180,3), (270,0), (360,3). Amplitude and period are correct and only the midline is wrong, by 2 squares, which is more than the one-grid-square tolerance. This is exactly what 'centred on the wrong midline' detects. Caveat: her peak at 6 is past the -5..5 grid and would clip at the edge, but the midline is still clearly off. The predicate is generic and also fires for a flat-out forgotten shift (midline 0), so this diagnosis is not exclusive. A midline at 3 is the signature of this specific mistake.

results.construction: Target y = 2 sin(theta) + 2 on 0..360 degrees: midline y = 2, amplitude 2, so the range is 0..4. Key points, drawn left to right in one stroke: (0,2) rising, (90,4) peak, (180,2), (270,0) trough, (360,2). Coefficients [2,2] are inside the sine limits and the curve fits inside -5..5. It is a single-valued stroke, so it passes the vertical line test.

predicates.why: fn is sine, so vertical-shift-wrong is in the can_emit list. A student who reads 2 sin(theta) + 2 as 2(sin(theta) + 2) draws a full-amplitude (2) sine centred on y = a*q = 4 instead of y = 2: (0,4), (90,6), (180,4), (270,2), (360,4). Only the midline is wrong, by 2 squares, which is more than the one-grid-square tolerance, so the predicate fires. Caveat: her peak at 6 is past the -5..5 grid and would clip at the edge, but the midline is still clearly off. The predicate is generic and also fires for a forgotten shift (midline 0). Here a = q, so a*q = 4 is also a+q or a squared, but the shift-times-a reading is the natural source of a midline at 4.

results.construction: One smooth left-to-right stroke tracing y = -4cos(theta) over 0 to 360 degrees, a reflected cosine with amplitude 4 and no vertical shift. Start at (0, -4), the minimum. Rise through (90, 0) to the maximum at (180, 4). Fall through (270, 0) and finish at (360, -4). One full period, one stroke, never doubling back in x, and every value stays inside -5..5 (the extremes are -4 and 4). Within about one grid square of the target, so this satisfies the instrument's limits.

predicates.why: The misconception is about how the student names the amplitude (saying -4 instead of 4). It does not change what a student draws. A student who reads the minus sign as part of the amplitude still starts the curve at -4 and draws the correct reflected cosine, so off-target would not fire for them. If such a student did draw an upright cosine, the cause would be a missed reflection or a different slip, not this naming error. The predicate is the generic fallback for any sketch that fails to follow the curve (wrong shape, wrong period, a sine instead of a cosine, a stray stroke). It would mostly fire for those other reasons, so it is not a reliable signal for this misconception.

results.construction: One smooth left-to-right stroke over 0 to 360 degrees: start at the minimum (0, -2), rise through the midline point (90, 1), reach the maximum (180, 4), fall back through (270, 1) and finish at (360, -2). The curve is a cosine reflected in its midline y = 1 (a = -3, q = 1), so it is a single-valued stroke that passes the vertical line test and covers the full domain. It stays inside the -5..5 band and each plotted point sits on a grid intersection, so it is within a grid square of the target.

predicates.why: Cosine does list off-target as an emittable predicate, so it can fire here. It is the generic catch-all for any sketch that does not follow the curve. It would fire for a sine curve, a wrong phase, a sloppy wobble or a mispositioned curve, as well as for an unreflected y = 3cos(theta) + 1 drawn from (0, 4). The claimed misconception is the student calling the amplitude -4 (here -3), which is a naming error about the word amplitude. It does not predict a particular wrong shape, because a student who states a negative amplitude can still draw the reflected curve correctly. A student who ignores the minus and draws the unreflected curve is possible but is only one of several off-target causes. Attributing every off-target sketch to this misconception would mostly rebut a mistake the student did not make.

results.construction: Since -1 <= cos(theta) <= 1, y = 2cos(theta) - 3 runs from 2(-1)-3 = -5 to 2(1)-3 = -1, and both values are attained (cos = -1 and cos = 1 occur). On the instrument (range [-6,6]), use interval mode with from = -5 and to = -1, both whole numbers inside the range, and set both ends FILLED (openFrom = false, openTo = false). This satisfies every limit.

predicates.why: This is an interval-mode predicate and it does fire for the claimed misconception's build. A student who finds the range of 2cos(theta) alone and never adds q builds [-2, 2], which is on the lattice and has endpoints other than -5 and -1. But the predicate is a catch-all ('endpoints are not the right ones'). It fires equally for [1, 5] (q added with the wrong sign), [-4, -2] (the factor 2 forgotten) and [-1, 1] (neither a nor q used). Those are equally plausible wrong builds for this equation, so most firings would come from other errors. Those students would be shown the refutation 'you left out the added number', which is wrong for them: the [1, 5] student did add q, and the [-4, -2] student did not forget q. Because the predicate cannot separate the claimed misconception from the other ways to get the endpoints wrong, I mark it false.

results.construction: Use interval mode on the [-6,6] line. Since -1 <= sin(theta) <= 1, y = 3sin(theta)+2 runs from 3(-1)+2 = -1 to 3(1)+2 = 5, and sin reaches both +-1, so y actually attains both values. Place the left endpoint at the lattice point -1 and the right endpoint at 5, and set both ends filled (included, <= on both sides). Both -1 and 5 are whole numbers inside the range, so the validator limits are satisfied.

predicates.why: The predicate is listed for interval mode and would fire on this question for any interval whose endpoints are not -1 and 5. A student who ignores q builds [-3, 3] (from -a to a), which does fire it. But the predicate is a catch-all with nothing in it that is specific to leaving out q. It fires just as readily for [-5, 1] (adds q with the wrong sign), [1, 3] (adds q but forgets to multiply by the amplitude 3), [0, 6] and others. Those students would be told they left out the added number when they did not. Since a wrong diagnosis hands a student the refutation of a mistake she did not make, this does not reliably map to mc:g10m6s7-1-3:ignores-added-number.
